### 4194. Assistant (2026-06-02 00:13:03 中国标准时间)

我的结论是：如果你要把统计方案往“更主流、更抗审稿”方向推，优先把 DMRT 换成 Tukey HSD；不建议为了“统一风格”把这两块再改成 Kruskal-Wallis + Dunn。

原因很直接。你当前 methods 已经写明，形态学和力学这两块先过了 Shapiro-Wilk 和 Levene，所以被当作参数性三组比较处理，见 [03_文章撰写/build_manuscript_en.py](03_文章撰写/build_manuscript_en.py#L904)。在这种前提下，ANOVA 之后最稳妥、最容易被高影响力期刊和审稿人接受的后续多重比较，通常是 Tukey HSD；DMRT 也不是错，但它比 Tukey 更少见、也更宽松，所以别人最容易追问的不是“你能不能用”，而是“为什么不用更标准的 Tukey”。对应代码层面，当前还在用 Duncan 的主要就是形态图和力学图，分别在 [02_可视化/Figure/MainFig1D_mammilla_quantification.py](02_可视化/Figure/MainFig1D_mammilla_quantification.py) 和 [02_可视化/Figure/MainFig6_mechanics_force_shear.py](02_可视化/Figure/MainFig6_mechanics_force_shear.py)。

我不建议把这两块改成 Kruskal-Wallis + Dunn，有两个原因。第一，你自己已经声明这些变量满足参数前提，这时硬切去非参数，会让方法学逻辑变得不连贯。第二，n 本来就不大，Kruskal-Wallis + Dunn 通常更保守，检验力只会更低，不会比 Tukey 更“高级”。所以如果要换，应该是 ANOVA 保留，只把 post hoc 从 DMRT 改成 Tukey。反过来，Fig.4 那些糖链系综和热点指标继续保留 Mann-Whitney / Wilcoxon 是对的，因为你已经把它们归类为不满足正态/齐性或属于相对 apo 参考值的 signed-rank 场景，见 [03_文章撰写/build_manuscript_en.py](03_文章撰写/build_manuscript_en.py#L909)。

还有一个更重要的提醒：比 DMRT 本身更像“审稿雷点”的，是形态学那块的样本层级。你 methods 里写的是每物种 n=9 subfragments，而且来自 one scanned fragment，见 [03_文章撰写/build_manuscript_en.py](03_文章撰写/build_manuscript_en.py#L687)。这会让严格一点的审稿人质疑伪重复或层级独立性。也就是说，即使你把 DMRT 换成 Tukey，如果不把这个层级关系解释清楚，统计部分仍然可能被追问；但如果两者只能先修一个，Tukey 是更稳的表层修补，层级独立性则是更根本的风险点。

简化成一句建议就是：  
保留现在的 Mann-Whitney / Wilcoxon；如果你想把参数性三组比较做得更像高 IF 期刊常见写法，就把 DMRT 改成 Tukey HSD，不要改成 Kruskal-Wallis + Dunn。

如果你要，我下一步可以直接做两种中的一种：
1. 只改文字：把 methods、figure legends、results 里所有 Duncan 表述改成 Tukey 版本，但先不动图。

(.venv) (base) PS D:\system_folder\Desktop\Work On> $abs = "Comparative eggshell studies have mostly resolved shared matrix proteins at the inventory or glycosite level, leaving unclear how matched glycan states on conserved proteins scale into shell structure and hatching mechanics. Here, we compared chicken, duck, and pigeon under a conserved egg-tooth interface and integrated micro-CT morphometry, eggshell-matrix proteomics, intact glycopeptide mass spectrometry, Re-Glyco structural modelling, electrostatic analysis, and finite-element simulation. Cross-species separation appeared first in mammillary-layer organisation, whereas the broad matrix-protein toolkit remained largely shared. Within that shared background, ovalbumin (OVAL) showed an ordered shift from High Mannose-dominant glycans in chicken to Neutral Complex/Hybrid-dominant glycans in duck and Sialylated Complex/Hybrid-dominant glycans in pigeon. These states predicted progressively stronger shielding of the Ca²⁺-relevant OVAL surface and were mirrored by a chicken-high versus duck/pigeon-low contrast in local hatching resistance. Together, the data place OVAL glycan state as a proximate molecular layer linking a chicken-like eggshell state to mammillary organisation and inside-out failure behaviour."; $w = (($abs -replace '[^A-Za-z0-9\-\+²]+',' ') -split '\s+' | Where-Object {$_ -ne ''}).Count; Write-Output "ABSTRACT_WORDS=$w"

NEUROSCIENCE
Human brain glycoform coregulation network and 
glycan modification alterations in Alzheimer’s disease
Qi Zhang1, Cheng Ma2, Lih- Shen Chin1, Sheng Pan2, Lian Li1*
Despite the importance of protein glycosylation to brain health, current knowledge of glycosylated proteoforms 
or glycoforms in human brain and their alterations in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is limited. Here, we report a 
proteome- wide glycoform profiling study of human AD and control brains using intact glycopeptide- based quan-
titative glycoproteomics coupled with systems biology. Our study identified more than 10,000 human brain N- 
glycoforms from nearly 1200 glycoproteins and uncovered disease signatures of altered glycoforms and glycan 
modifications, including reduced sialylation and N-  glycan branching and elongation as well as elevated manno -
sylation and N- glycan truncation in AD. Network analyses revealed a higher- order organization of brain glycopro-
teome into networks of coregulated glycoforms and glycans and discovered glycoform and glycan modules 
associated with AD clinical phenotype, amyloid- β accumulation, and tau pathology. Our findings provide valuable 
insights into disease pathogenesis and a rich resource of glycoform and glycan changes in AD and pave the way 
forward for developing glycosylation- based therapies and biomarkers for AD.
INTRODUCTION
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, 
characterized pathologically by accumulation of amyloid- β (Aβ ) 
plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles in the brain (1, 2). Genome- 
wide association studies (GW AS) have identified over 40 genetic risk 
loci for AD (3 , 4), and transcriptomic and proteomic analyses re-
vealed RNA and protein expression changes that are much broader 
than Aβ and tau accumulation in AD brain (3 , 5). However, DNA 
variations and RNA or protein level changes alone are insufficient to 
account for all aspects of AD pathobiology, as proteins are known to 
undergo posttranslational modifications that control their function 
(6, 7) and proteoforms generated from protein modifications add 
enormous diversity and complexity to the proteome (7 ). The most 
prevalent and complex form of protein modification is glycosylation, 
which produces vastly diverse arrays of glycosylated proteoforms or 
glycoforms (a glycoform is an isoform of a protein that differs only 
with respect to the number or type of attached glycan) to greatly ex-
pand the proteome and its functionalities (8, 9).
As a major type of glycosylation, N- linked glycosylation controls 
many biological processes through covalent attachment of glycans to 
asparagine residues of proteins (9, 10). Protein N- glycosylation in-
volves a multi- step process that begins by oligosaccharyltransferase 
(OST)–catalyzed “en bloc” addition of a 14- sugar precursor Glc3Man9 
GlcNAc2 to asparagine residues within the sequon N- X- S|T (X  ≠ P) 
of newly synthesized proteins in the lumen of endoplasmic reticulum 
(ER). The N- glycans are then processed and remodeled by coordi-
nated actions of glycosyltransferases and glycosidases in the ER 
and Golgi compartments, producing a wide variety of glycoforms 
with distinct glycan compositions and structures, such as oligoman-
nose, hybrid, and complex- type N- glycans (9, 11). The site- specific N- 
glycans on glycoproteins not only regulate protein folding, activity, 
trafficking, and subcellular localization but also serve as the sugar 
code to mediate bio- recognition and signal distinct cellular outcomes 
(8, 12).
N- glycan modifications of proteins are vital for the development, 
maintenance, and function of the nervous system (13, 14). The im-
portance of protein N- glycosylation to brain health is underscored 
by the findings that genetic mutations in glycosylation enzymes for 
N- glycan attachment or processing cause human congenital disor -
ders with prominent neurological abnormalities (15). N- glycans on 
glycoproteins are increasingly recognized as functional effectors 
of genetic and epigenetic disease risk (16). Accumulating evidence 
points to a link between aberrant protein N- glycosylation and AD 
pathogenesis (17–19). Glycomic analyses of N- glycans detached from 
glycoproteins have revealed changes in global levels of N- glycans 
in AD brains (20–22), but the information of glycoproteins and gly-
cosites bearing the N- glycans was lost. We recently performed an 
integrated proteomic and glycoproteomic study using 18O- tagging to 
label in vivo N- glycosylation sites and identified disease- associated 
N- glycoproteins and glycosites with altered N- glycosylation site oc-
cupancy in AD brains (23). While 1132 unique N- glycoproteins were 
analyzed, the study was limited by the use of a deglycosylation step in 
the workflow, resulting in the loss of information on glycans at each 
glycosite. A more recent intact glycopeptide- based glycoproteomic 
study reported qualitative analysis of site- specific N- glycan and gly-
coforms from 268 unique N- glycoproteins (defined by unique gene 
ID) in AD and control brains (24), but suffered from the low cover-
age of brain N- glycoproteome and the lack of quantitative informa-
tion regarding the levels of site- specific N- glycans and glycoforms in 
human brain and their alterations in AD. Because of the inherent 
complexity of N- glycan modifications and technical challenges in 
intact glycoproteomics and associated data analysis, our current 
knowledge of system- wide changes in human brain glycoforms and 
site- specific N- glycan modifications in AD is very limited.
Here, we established an integrated approach that combines intact 
glycopeptide- based quantitative glycoproteomics and systems biolo-
gy for large- scale, in- depth analysis of glycoforms and site- specific N- 
glycan modifications in human brain and their changes in AD. Using 
this approach, we identified more than 10,000 N- glycoforms from 
1184 unique N- glycoproteins and obtained a system- level view of

human brain glycoforms and their attached N- glycans. Our analyses 
reveal previously unknown changes in glycoforms and site- specific 
glycans in AD and uncover glycoform and glycan coregulation net-
works in human brain and their alterations in AD. Our findings pro-
vide mechanistic insights into the roles of N- glycan modifications in 
brain dysfunction in AD and establish a framework of glycosylation- 
based networks and pathways for understanding and treating AD.
RESUL TS
Glycoproteomic landscape of AD and control brains revealed 
by intact glycoproteomics
To characterize human brain glycoproteome and its changes in AD, 
we established and optimized a mass spectrometry–based intact 
glycoproteomics platform for large- scale simultaneous profiling of 
glycoproteins, glycoforms, glycosites, and site- specific glycan compo-
sitions in brain samples. Our glycoproteomics workflow consisted of 
SDS- mediated protein extraction (25), filter- aided sample prepara-
tion (FASP) (26), glycopeptide enrichment by strong anion exchange 
and electrostatic repulsion–hydrophilic interaction chromatography 
(SAX- ERLIC) (27), liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrom-
etry (LC- MS/MS) with higher- energy collisional dissociation (HCD) 
using a stepped collision energy (SCE) setting (28), and MS data 
analysis using Byonic software (29) for the identification of intact 
N- glycopeptides and their attached glycan compositions. Because 
correct assignment of glycopeptides carrying glycan compositions 
with similar masses [e.g., one sialic acid (NeuAc) versus two fucoses, 
Δm  =  1.0204 Da] is a challenge in glycoproteomics, we used the 
Byonic 182 human N- glycan library, which does not contain glycan 
compositions with more than one fucose, to minimize the false as-
signment of NeuAc- containing glycan compositions to fucosylated 
glycan compositions containing two or more fucoses. Byonic weights 
diagnostic peaks at mass/charge ratio (m/z) 292.103 for NeuAc and 
274.092 for NeuAc with water loss very heavily for the assignment of 
NeuAc- containing glycopeptides (29, 30). The glycopeptide assign-
ment was verified by manual validation with the evidence of diagnos-
tic oxonium ions and the monoisotopic precursor ion profile (fig. S1). 
Furthermore, analysis of technical replicates from control brain sam-
ples confirmed that the coverage and reproducibility of our glycopro-
teomics analyses are acceptable for glycoproteome- profiling studies 
(fig. S2). We used the optimized glycoproteomics workflow to analyze 
human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex tissue samples from the same 
cohort of 16 neuropathologically confirmed AD and control cases 
(table S1) as in our proteomics and glycosite- profiling studies (23, 31). 
In total, we identified 12,176 unique N- glycopeptides with attached 
N- glycans at the N- X- S|T (X  ≠ P) sequon, corresponding to 10,731 
unique N- glycoforms with 164 distinct N- glycan compositions at 
2544 unique N- glycosites in 1184 unique N- glycoproteins (Fig. 1, A to 
D, and table S2). This dataset represents the largest glycoproteome da-
taset of human AD and control brains to date with site- specific N- 
glycan and glycoform information.
Comparison of the glycoproteome dataset with our proteome 
profiling data from the same cohort (31) showed that 348 glycopro-
teins (~29%) of the 1184 glycoproteins were exclusively identified by 
intact glycoproteomics (Fig. 1E), demonstrating that our glycopro-
teomics workflow enables analysis of a subset of proteins that may 
otherwise remain undetected by global proteome profiling. As ex-
pected, the glycoproteome dataset was enriched for plasma mem-
brane and extracellular proteins, lysosomal and ER lumenal proteins, 
neuronal and synaptic membrane proteins as well as receptors, ion 
channels, and cell adhesion molecules (fig.  S3 and table  S3). Our 
analyses (Fig. 1, E and F) showed that ~51% of the N- glycoproteins 
and 41% of the N- glycosites identified in this study overlapped with 
those detected in our previous study (23) using a deglycosylation- 
based glycoproteomic approach (deglycoproteomics). The differ -
ences in the identifications of glycoproteins and glycosites between 
this work and our prior study are likely due to the differences in 
glycopeptide enrichment and MS fragmentation methods used 
in intact glycoproteomics versus deglycoproteomics analyses. 
Matching our intact glycoproteomic dataset to the UniProt database 
showed that 65% of the identified 2544 N- glycosites were annotated 
or predicted in the database (Fig. 1G). The current study provided 
experimental evidence for more than 950 UniProt- predicted N- 
glycosites and identified more than 880 N- glycosites that have not 
been previously reported in UniProt (Fig. 1G). Comparison of our 
glycoproteomic data with the results of Suttapitugsakul et  al. (24) 
and Tena et al. (32) showed substantial overlaps in the identified N- 
glycoproteins, N- glycosites, N- glycans, and N- glycoforms (fig. S4). 
Notably, our glycoproteomics workflow achieved a greater coverage 
of brain glycoproteome, enabling analysis of additional 9597 N-  
glycoforms, 892 N- glycoproteins, 2007 N- glycosites, and 45 N-  
glycan compositions in this work (fig. S4).
Our glycoproteomic analysis identified 7772 N- glycoforms in con-
trol and 8196 N- glycoforms in AD, with 5237 N- glycoforms overlap-
ping between control and AD brains (Fig.  1D and table  S2). We 
identified 164 N- glycan compositions in both control and AD brains 
(table S2) and categorized them into seven glycan types: oligoman-
nose, paucimannose, chitobiose core, undecorated complex/hybrid 
(neither fucosylated nor sialylated), fucosylated- only, sialylated- only, 
and sialofucosylated (sialylated and fucosylated) glycans. In control 
brains, ~36% of the total N- glycoforms carried oligomannose- type 
glycans and ~41% carried fucose- containing glycans (including both 
fucosylated- only glycans and sialofucosylated glycans) (Fig. 1H and 
fig. S5A), consistent with the findings from previous glycoproteomic 
and glycomic studies (20, 24, 33). In addition, ~26% of control brain 
glycoforms carried sialic acid–containing glycans (including both 
sialylated- only glycans and sialofucosylated glycans), ~8% carried un-
decorated complex/hybrid (neither fucosylated nor sialylated) gly-
cans, ~4% carried paucimannose- type glycans, and ~ 2% carried 
chitobiose core–type glycans (Fig. 1H and fig. S5A). We found that 
the percentages of sialylated- only glycoforms, sialofucosylated glyco-
forms, and total sialylated glycoforms were significantly decreased in 
AD brains, whereas the percentages of fucosylated- only glycoforms 
and undecorated complex/hybrid glycoforms were significantly in-
creased in AD (Fig. 1H). To gain insight into N- glycan branching, we 
classified the N- glycans into different branching categories based on 
the number of antennary HexNAc residues (i.e., total number of 
HexNAc residues − 2) in glycan compositions (Fig. 1H). We note that 
these branching categories are putative structural assignments be-
cause a single glycan composition may represent multiple glycan 
structures and branching types (34). Our analysis revealed that the 
percentages of glycoforms carrying glycans with a total of six HexNAc 
residues (assigned tetra- antennary glycans) or >6 HexNAc residues 
(highly branched or elongated glycans) were significantly decreased 
in AD brains (Fig. 1H).
We identified 1952 N- glycosites in control and 2114 N- glycosites 
in AD brains, with 1522 N- glycosites shared by control and AD 
brains (Fig.  1C, and table  S2). Approximately 57% of the total

NEUROSCIENCE
Human brain glycoform coregulation network and 
glycan modification alterations in Alzheimer’s disease
Qi Zhang1, Cheng Ma2, Lih- Shen Chin1, Sheng Pan2, Lian Li1*
Despite the importance of protein glycosylation to brain health, current knowledge of glycosylated proteoforms 
or glycoforms in human brain and their alterations in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is limited. Here, we report a 
proteome- wide glycoform profiling study of human AD and control brains using intact glycopeptide- based quan-
titative glycoproteomics coupled with systems biology. Our study identified more than 10,000 human brain N- 
glycoforms from nearly 1200 glycoproteins and uncovered disease signatures of altered glycoforms and glycan 
modifications, including reduced sialylation and N-  glycan branching and elongation as well as elevated manno -
sylation and N- glycan truncation in AD. Network analyses revealed a higher- order organization of brain glycopro-
teome into networks of coregulated glycoforms and glycans and discovered glycoform and glycan modules 
associated with AD clinical phenotype, amyloid- β accumulation, and tau pathology. Our findings provide valuable 
insights into disease pathogenesis and a rich resource of glycoform and glycan changes in AD and pave the way 
forward for developing glycosylation- based therapies and biomarkers for AD.
INTRODUCTION
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, 
characterized pathologically by accumulation of amyloid- β (Aβ ) 
plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles in the brain (1, 2). Genome- 
wide association studies (GW AS) have identified over 40 genetic risk 
loci for AD (3 , 4), and transcriptomic and proteomic analyses re-
vealed RNA and protein expression changes that are much broader 
than Aβ and tau accumulation in AD brain (3 , 5). However, DNA 
variations and RNA or protein level changes alone are insufficient to 
account for all aspects of AD pathobiology, as proteins are known to 
undergo posttranslational modifications that control their function 
(6, 7) and proteoforms generated from protein modifications add 
enormous diversity and complexity to the proteome (7 ). The most 
prevalent and complex form of protein modification is glycosylation, 
which produces vastly diverse arrays of glycosylated proteoforms or 
glycoforms (a glycoform is an isoform of a protein that differs only 
with respect to the number or type of attached glycan) to greatly ex-
pand the proteome and its functionalities (8, 9).
As a major type of glycosylation, N- linked glycosylation controls 
many biological processes through covalent attachment of glycans to 
asparagine residues of proteins (9, 10). Protein N- glycosylation in-
volves a multi- step process that begins by oligosaccharyltransferase 
(OST)–catalyzed “en bloc” addition of a 14- sugar precursor Glc3Man9 
GlcNAc2 to asparagine residues within the sequon N- X- S|T (X  ≠ P) 
of newly synthesized proteins in the lumen of endoplasmic reticulum 
(ER). The N- glycans are then processed and remodeled by coordi-
nated actions of glycosyltransferases and glycosidases in the ER 
and Golgi compartments, producing a wide variety of glycoforms 
with distinct glycan compositions and structures, such as oligoman-
nose, hybrid, and complex- type N- glycans (9, 11). The site- specific N- 
glycans on glycoproteins not only regulate protein folding, activity, 
trafficking, and subcellular localization but also serve as the sugar 
code to mediate bio- recognition and signal distinct cellular outcomes 
(8, 12).
N- glycan modifications of proteins are vital for the development, 
maintenance, and function of the nervous system (13, 14). The im-
portance of protein N- glycosylation to brain health is underscored 
by the findings that genetic mutations in glycosylation enzymes for 
N- glycan attachment or processing cause human congenital disor -
ders with prominent neurological abnormalities (15). N- glycans on 
glycoproteins are increasingly recognized as functional effectors 
of genetic and epigenetic disease risk (16). Accumulating evidence 
points to a link between aberrant protein N- glycosylation and AD 
pathogenesis (17–19). Glycomic analyses of N- glycans detached from 
glycoproteins have revealed changes in global levels of N- glycans 
in AD brains (20–22), but the information of glycoproteins and gly-
cosites bearing the N- glycans was lost. We recently performed an 
integrated proteomic and glycoproteomic study using 18O- tagging to 
label in vivo N- glycosylation sites and identified disease- associated 
N- glycoproteins and glycosites with altered N- glycosylation site oc-
cupancy in AD brains (23). While 1132 unique N- glycoproteins were 
analyzed, the study was limited by the use of a deglycosylation step in 
the workflow, resulting in the loss of information on glycans at each 
glycosite. A more recent intact glycopeptide- based glycoproteomic 
study reported qualitative analysis of site- specific N- glycan and gly-
coforms from 268 unique N- glycoproteins (defined by unique gene 
ID) in AD and control brains (24), but suffered from the low cover-
age of brain N- glycoproteome and the lack of quantitative informa-
tion regarding the levels of site- specific N- glycans and glycoforms in 
human brain and their alterations in AD. Because of the inherent 
complexity of N- glycan modifications and technical challenges in 
intact glycoproteomics and associated data analysis, our current 
knowledge of system- wide changes in human brain glycoforms and 
site- specific N- glycan modifications in AD is very limited.
Here, we established an integrated approach that combines intact 
glycopeptide- based quantitative glycoproteomics and systems biolo-
gy for large- scale, in- depth analysis of glycoforms and site- specific N- 
glycan modifications in human brain and their changes in AD. Using 
this approach, we identified more than 10,000 N- glycoforms from 
1184 unique N- glycoproteins and obtained a system- level view of

reveal previously unknown changes in glycoforms and site- specific 
glycans in AD and uncover glycoform and glycan coregulation net-

vide mechanistic insights into the roles of N- glycan modifications in 
brain dysfunction in AD and establish a framework of glycosylation- 
based networks and pathways for understanding and treating AD.

by intact glycoproteomics
To characterize human brain glycoproteome and its changes in AD, 
we established and optimized a mass spectrometry–based intact 
glycoproteomics platform for large- scale simultaneous profiling of 
glycoproteins, glycoforms, glycosites, and site- specific glycan compo-
sitions in brain samples. Our glycoproteomics workflow consisted of 
SDS- mediated protein extraction (25), filter- aided sample prepara-
tion (FASP) (26), glycopeptide enrichment by strong anion exchange 
and electrostatic repulsion–hydrophilic inter

(.venv) (base) PS D:\system_folder\Desktop\Work On\03_文章撰写> function Replace-BodySegment {
>>     param(
>>         [string]$Path,
>>         [string]$StartMarker,
>>         [string]$EndMarker,
>>         [hashtable]$Patterns
>>     )
>> 
>>     $raw = Get-Content -Raw -Path $Path
>>     $start = $raw.IndexOf($StartMarker)
>>     $end = $raw.IndexOf($EndMarker)
>>     if ($start -lt 0 -or $end -lt 0 -or $end -le $start) {
>>         throw "Marker not found or invalid range in $Path"
>>     }
>> 
>>     Copy-Item -Path $Path -Destination ($Path + '.bak') -Force
>> 
>>     $prefix = $raw.Substring(0, $start)
>>     $body = $raw.Substring($start, $end - $start)
>>     $suffix = $raw.Substring($end)
>> 
>>     foreach ($k in $Patterns.Keys) {
>>         $body = [regex]::Replace($body, $k, $Patterns[$k])
>>     }
>> 
>>     $newRaw = $prefix + $body + $suffix
>>     if ($newRaw.Length -lt 20000) {
>>         throw "Safety check failed: output too short for $Path"
>>     }
>> 
>>     Set-Content -Path $Path -Value $newRaw -Encoding UTF8
>> }

>> """
>> Strict Chinese translation generator.
>> Produces a sentence-aligned Chinese manuscript from the latest English manuscript.
>> """
>> 
>> from pathlib import Path
>> import re
>> import time
>> from docx import Document
>> from docx.oxml.ns import qn
>> from docx.oxml import OxmlElement
>> from deep_translator import GoogleTranslator
>> 
>> EN_DOC = Path(__file__).with_name("manuscript260602v2.docx")
>> OUT_DOC = Path(__file__).with_name("manuscript260602v2_cn.docx")
>> 
>> translator = GoogleTranslator(source="en", target="zh-CN")
>> _cache: dict[str, str] = {}
>> 
>> 
>> def _has_english_letters(text: str) -> bool:
>>     return bool(re.search(r"[A-Za-z]", text))
>> 
>> 
>> def _should_translate(text: str) -> bool:
>>     t = text.strip()
>>     if not t:
>>         return False
>>     if not _has_english_letters(t):
>>         return False
>>     if re.fullmatch(r"[\d\s.,;:()\[\]{}\-+/×=]+", t):
>>         return False
>>     return True
>> 
>> 
>> def _translate_text(text: str, retries: int = 3) -> str:
>>     if text in _cache:
>>         return _cache[text]
>> 
>>     last_err = None
>>     for i in range(retries):
>>         try:
>>             out = translator.translate(text)
>>             if not out:
>>                 out = text
>>             _cache[text] = out
>>             return out
>>         except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
>>             last_err = e
>>             time.sleep(0.8 * (i + 1))
>> 
>>     # Fallback: keep original if remote translation fails.
>>     print(f"[WARN] translation failed, keep original: {text[:80]} :: {last_err}")
>>     _cache[text] = text
>>     return text
>> 
>> 
>> def _replace_paragraph_text_keep_format(p, new_text: str) -> None:
>>     if p.runs:
>>         p.runs[0].text = new_text
>>         for r in p.runs[1:]:
>>             r.text = ""
>>     else:
>>         p.add_run(new_text)
>> 
>> 
>> def _set_cn_fonts(doc: Document) -> None:
>>     # Ensure East Asian fonts render consistently in translated output.
>>     for para in doc.paragraphs:
>>         for run in para.runs:
>>             run.font.name = "Times New Roman"
>>             rPr = run._r.get_or_add_rPr()
>>             rFonts = rPr.find(qn("w:rFonts"))
>>             if rFonts is None:
>>                 rFonts = OxmlElement("w:rFonts")
>>                 rPr.insert(0, rFonts)
>>             rFonts.set(qn("w:ascii"), "Times New Roman")
>>             rFonts.set(qn("w:hAnsi"), "Times New Roman")
>>             rFonts.set(qn("w:cs"), "Times New Roman")
>>             rFonts.set(qn("w:eastAsia"), "SimSun")
>> 
>> 
>> def _translate_paragraphs(paragraphs) -> int:
>>     changed = 0
>>     for p in paragraphs:
>>         src = "".join(r.text for r in p.runs) if p.runs else p.text
>>         if not _should_translate(src):
>>             continue
>>         dst = _translate_text(src)
>>         _replace_paragraph_text_keep_format(p, dst)
>>         changed += 1
>>     return changed
>> 
>> 
>> def main() -> None:
>>     if not EN_DOC.exists():
>>         raise FileNotFoundError(f"English manuscript not found: {EN_DOC}")
>> 
>>     doc = Document(str(EN_DOC))
>>     changed = 0
>> 
>>     changed += _translate_paragraphs(doc.paragraphs)
>> 
>>     for table in doc.tables:
>>         for row in table.rows:
>>             for cell in row.cells:
>>                 changed += _translate_paragraphs(cell.paragraphs)
>> 
>>     for sec in doc.sections:
>>         changed += _translate_paragraphs(sec.header.paragraphs)
>>         changed += _translate_paragraphs(sec.footer.paragraphs)
>> 
>>     _set_cn_fonts(doc)
>>     doc.save(str(OUT_DOC))
>>     print(f"[OK] translated paragraphs: {changed}")
>>     print(f"[OK] {OUT_DOC}")
>> 
>> 
>> if __name__ == "__main__":
>>     main()
>> '@ | Set-Content -Path "./build_manuscript_cn.py" -Encoding UTF8
